title: Lesson 68: Computer-Use Agents: Browser Automation, Safety, and Guardrails
description: How a computer-use agent operates a screen through a perceive-think-act loop, the three ways it can see a page, why prompt injection is the defining risk of browser automation, and the guardrail stack that keeps an agent from doing damage while it clicks.

questions.question: What structural property of a computer-use agent makes it possible to place guardrails between the model and the real world?
options: The model returns a proposed action that a control layer in your code performs.
The model performs each mouse and keyboard action directly on the screen itself.
The model is prevented from reading any of the page content it might later act on.
The agent only runs on pages that contain no visual elements at all.
questions.explanation: The model only proposes; your control layer decides whether to carry the action out. That separation is where guardrails, approval gates, and allowlists live, so the model never touches the machine directly.

questions.question: An agent struggles on a JavaScript-heavy page where the page structure is noisy but the screen is clear. Which approach fits best?
options: Use only the accessibility tree, since it always reflects everything on the page.
Use only full screenshots, since the structured signal can never help on any page.
Use the structured signal, falling back to screenshots when it runs out.
Disable the step cap so the agent can keep retrying the same click forever.
questions.explanation: The hybrid approach defaults to the cheap structured signal, such as the accessibility tree or DOM, and falls back to screenshots on visual or noisy pages. Routing per task beats committing to a single way of seeing.

questions.question: Why is browser automation more exposed to prompt injection than a tool call you wrote yourself?
options: Browsers automatically strip all embedded text out of a page before a model can read it.
The page content the agent must read can itself carry hidden instructions.
Injected instructions can only ever change a chat answer and never a real action.
Web pages are always authored by the same user who asked the agent to visit them.
questions.explanation: A tool call has a defined shape you control, but a browsing agent must read the web, and the content it reads is the same channel an attacker can use to give it orders. That is why its guardrails assume content is untrusted rather than relying on the model to ignore attacks.
